title: The Numbers Every Programmer Should Know
subtitle: Your CPU is blindingly fast — so why is software ever slow? Because not all memory is equal, and the gaps between them are staggering.
hook: Yesterday we saw the CPU rip through instructions billions of times a second. So why does anything ever feel slow? Here's the secret that separates people who *write* code from people who make it *fast*: the CPU spends most of its life **waiting** — for data to arrive from memory. And the difference in wait times between the fastest and slowest storage isn't 2x or 10x. It's roughly the difference between a **second and a decade**. Internalize these gaps and you'll understand performance, caching, and half of systems design.

sections.heading: The memory hierarchy
sections.body:
There isn't one kind of memory — there's a **hierarchy**, trading speed for size and cost. Near the CPU sit tiny, blisteringly-fast stores; far away sit huge, slow ones:

- **CPU registers / L1 cache** — tiny, essentially instant.
- **L2 / L3 cache** — small, very fast.
- **RAM (main memory)** — gigabytes, but ~100x slower than cache.
- **SSD** — huge, but far slower than RAM.
- **Network / disk far away** — enormous, and glacial by comparison.

The CPU can only compute on data that's close. If the data it needs is far down the hierarchy, it stalls — doing nothing — until it arrives.

sections.label: The gaps, scaled to human time
sections.body: Multiply every real latency by ~a billion so it's human-readable. **L1 cache = 1 second.** RAM = a couple of **minutes**. An SSD read = a few **days**. A spinning disk seek = a few **months**. A network round-trip across the world = **years**. Same units, wildly different worlds. When your program is slow, it's almost never 'too much math' — it's waiting on the far end of this ladder.

sections.caption: Closer to the CPU = faster but smaller. Every step down is a large jump in latency, which is why *where* your data lives dominates performance.

sections.heading: Locality: the trick that saves us
sections.body:
The reason computers aren't hopelessly slow is a pattern called **locality of reference**: programs tend to reuse the same data (temporal locality) and data stored near it (spatial locality). Hardware bets on this by **caching** — quietly keeping recently- and nearby-used data in the fast tiers.

So the practical lesson for building anything fast: **keep the data you need close, and touch it in predictable patterns.** Looping over a compact array is fast because it streams neatly into cache; chasing pointers all over memory is slow because every jump risks a trip down the hierarchy. This single idea — mind where your data lives — reappears in caching, databases, and distributed systems throughout this track.

takeaways: The CPU is fast, so real-world slowness is usually **waiting for data**, not computing.
Memory is a **hierarchy**: registers/cache → RAM → SSD → network, trading speed for size.
The latency gaps are enormous — scaled up, L1 ≈ 1 second while a global network hop ≈ years.
**Locality of reference** (reusing recent/nearby data) lets caching hide most of the cost.
To go fast: keep needed data **close** and access it in **predictable patterns** (arrays beat pointer-chasing).

quiz.q: If a modern program feels slow, what's the most common underlying cause?
options: The CPU can't do the math fast enough
It's waiting on data from slower tiers of the memory hierarchy
quiz.explain: CPUs are extremely fast at arithmetic; the usual bottleneck is stalling while data travels up from RAM, disk, or the network.

quiz.q: Roughly how does RAM latency compare to L1 cache latency?
quiz.explain: RAM is on the order of 100x slower than L1 cache — scaled to human time, seconds vs. minutes. That's why keeping hot data in cache matters so much.

quiz.q: What does 'locality of reference' let hardware do?
options: Cache recently- and nearby-used data in fast tiers, since programs tend to reuse it
quiz.explain: Programs reuse recent data (temporal) and nearby data (spatial), so caches keep that data close — hiding most of the latency ladder.
